data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Preferring the better-corroborated theory is defensible on Popper's terms as a non-inductive, critical preference for the theory with the highest surviving informative content, but accepting this costs us any guarantee of future success or probability of truth, reducing rational action to a bold conjecture that the unrefuted parts of the theory will hold in the new domain.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the preference relies on an assumption that the future will resemble the past (uniformity of nature), it smuggles in induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the preference claims to increase the probability of the theory being true, it contradicts Popper's rejection of probabilistic confirmation.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the preference cannot distinguish between a theory that survived trivial tests and one that survived severe tests, it fails to capture 'corroboration'.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the preference implies we are justified in believing the theory will work, rather than just hoping it will, it reverts to justificationism.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism is 'Critical Preference via Informational Content': Corroboration reports the severity of tests survived relative to the theory's logical improbability (information content). We prefer the highly corroborated theory not because it is likely true (induction), but because it has withstood attempts to eliminate its high informational content. The preference is a methodological rule to act on the best-tested error-elimination candidate, acknowledging that this choice itself is falsifiable if the theory fails in the novel domain.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
